query: For high-entropy-alloy protective coatings in wear-resistant applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their wear performance and why? Define a controlled change that would distinguish the hypothesis from a baseline, the directional observations expected if it is correct, the range over which it should hold, the prior evidence that supports it, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The wear performance of high-entropy alloy (HEA) protective coatings is primarily governed by the in-situ formation of a continuous, mechanically robust oxide layer that acts as a self-lubricating barrier against abrasive and adhesive wear. In oxidizing environments, this oxide film forms uniformly on a homogeneous HEA coating, distributing contact stresses and reducing direct metal contact during friction.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogeneous HEA coating (e.g., AlCoCrFeNi-based) prepared with minimal pre-existing oxide layers and a uniform microstructure.
generation.intervention: Subject the HEA coating to wear testing under a controlled oxidizing atmosphere (ambient air) versus an inert atmosphere (e.g., argon or vacuum) to promote versus suppress oxide formation, respectively.
generation.conditions: Wear tests conducted over a range of temperatures (room temperature up to 800 °C) and identical mechanical loads, ensuring that environmental oxygen availability is the only variable.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline or lamellar oxide film that is well adhered to the coating surface and uniformly distributed across the wear track.
generation.mechanism: The oxide film acts as a protective barrier by redistributing contact stresses and reducing metal-to-metal asperity contact, thereby lowering friction and wear. In oxidizing conditions, the controlled oxide growth enhances wear resistance compared to inert conditions where no such film develops.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under oxidizing conditions, the HEA coating will develop a uniform oxide layer, resulting in lower friction coefficients and reduced wear rates compared to the same coating tested in an inert atmosphere. Furthermore, beyond a certain oxygen availability threshold, additional oxidation should not lead to further improvement, indicating a saturation effect.
generation.baseline: Wear testing of identical HEA coatings under an inert atmosphere where minimal or no oxide film formation is expected.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold for HEA coatings with homogeneous microstructures and phase compositions in applications up to 800 °C. It may not apply if the alloy has significant microstructural defects, large phase separations, or if the oxide scale becomes too thick or brittle.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative details of oxide film thickness, its precise composition, and the stress distribution characteristics remain to be fully characterized, and the influence of minor alloying variations on oxide layer formation is not yet well understood.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical HEA coatings. Conduct wear tests under identical loads and temperatures, one set in an oxidizing atmosphere (ambient air) and the other in an inert atmosphere (argon or vacuum). Characterize the worn surfaces using SEM/EDS and XPS to analyze oxide film formation and measure wear rates and friction coefficients.
measurements: Oxide film thickness and composition (via SEM/EDS and XPS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HEA coatings tested under inert conditions display wear rates, friction coefficients, and surface characteristics (including lack of a protective oxide film) comparable to those tested in oxidizing conditions, then the hypothesis that a robust oxide film governs enhanced wear resistance would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractSustained wear damages on the sliding surfaces of alloys are generally the culprit responsible for the failure of various mechanical systems. Inspired by high-entropy effects, here we deliberately deploy nanohierarchical architecture with composition undulation in a Ni50(AlNbTiV)50 complex concentrated alloy, which yields ultralow wear rate within the order of 10−7 to 10−6 mm3/Nm between room temperature and 800 °C. Such remarkable wear resistance heretofore represents one of the highest wear resistance reported for the bulk alloys or composites, and originates from the multi-type adaptive friction interface protection governed by intrinsically nano-coupled grains and nanoprecipitates. This cooperative heterostructure releases gradient frictional stress in stages upon wear at room temperature through the coexistence of multiple deformation pathways while activating a dense nanocrystalline glaze layer upon wear at 800 °C to minimize adhesive and oxidative wear. Our work uncovers a practical avenue for tailoring wear properties with multicomponent heterostructures over a wide temperature range.
